problem: The trap tells students that a bus cable break 'splits the bus' and that 'nodes on one part may still work'. Standard textbooks say the opposite for a bus: a break in the backbone removes termination, causes reflections and stops all transmission, even between devices on the same side of the break. A student who writes the trap's version in an exam loses marks.
fix: Reword: 'Assuming a bus cable break only affects part of the network: on a plain bus with one terminated backbone cable, a break or fault usually stops all transmission on the whole bus, because the cut end reflects signals. Splitting into working parts needs repeaters, bridges or separate segments.' Keep the body wording 'can split or kill the bus' only if it says the split case needs such devices.

problem: The symbol n changes meaning. In the mesh formulas n is the total number of nodes, but in the star row of the table (and the star paragraph) n counts only the end devices, so the switch is not counted. A student who uses n = total nodes for a star gets n − 1 cables and n − 1 central ports.
fix: State the meaning in each case: 'for mesh, n = total nodes; for star, bus and ring, n = number of end nodes, not counting the central switch or the backbone'.

problem: It says adding a node to a full mesh needs 'n new cables and n new ports across the old nodes', but the new node also needs n ports of its own, and the total port count is not mentioned. The sentence understates the cost.
fix: Say: adding a node to a mesh of n nodes needs n new cables, one new port on each old node, and n ports on the new node, so ports grow as n².
